title: Harry Innes
summary: Virginia lawyer Harry Innes came to Kentucky as a judge, sat in eight statehood conventions, and in 1789 became the state’s first U.S. district judge.
bodyMarkdown:
[Harry Innes](/people/#harry-innes) was born in Caroline County, Virginia, in 1752, the son of an Anglican rector. He studied at the College of William & Mary, read law under George Wythe, and opened a practice in Bedford County on the Virginia frontier. During the Revolution he managed the Chiswell lead mines on the New River for Virginia's patriot government, a job that kept the army supplied with bullets.

In 1782 the Virginia legislature chose him as an assistant judge of the new supreme court for the District of Kentucky. He was sworn in at Crow's Station, near present-day Danville, that November and moved west in 1783. From 1784 to 1789 he served as attorney general for the district.

Kentucky's leaders spent most of that decade arguing about how to break away from Virginia. Innes sat in eight of the ten conventions held at [Danville](/stories/danville-and-constitution-square/) to work out statehood. He was frustrated with how slowly Congress and Virginia moved, and he was linked with men who talked with Spanish officials about trade on the Mississippi. He denied ever plotting to separate Kentucky from the Union, and historians still weigh how far those talks went.

On September 26, 1789, [George Washington](/people/#george-washington) appointed him the first United States district judge for Kentucky. Innes held the seat for twenty-seven years. In 1806 Joseph Hamilton Daveiss brought charges against [Aaron Burr](/people/#aaron-burr) in Innes's court in Frankfort, and Innes presided over those hearings, in which Burr was not indicted. For years afterward he fought libel suits and attacks from Humphrey Marshall, who accused him of the Spanish intrigue.

Off the bench, Innes farmed, speculated in land, served as a Transylvania University trustee, and built one of the finest private libraries in Kentucky. He died in [Frankfort](/stories/frankfort-franks-ford-becomes-the-capital/) on September 20, 1816.

## Kentucky today

Innes is buried in Frankfort Cemetery, on the hill above the Kentucky capital.
